description: Functions, sources, deficiency and excess for protein, fats and carbohydrates, plus protein complementation.
content_html:
What Are Macronutrients?

Macronutrients are the nutrients your body needs in large quantities every day. They supply energy and build or repair tissues. All three — protein, fats and carbohydrates — appear on every nutrition label and form the backbone of every meal you cook. Compare them with micronutrients (vitamins and minerals), which are needed in tiny amounts and do not supply energy. Getting the distinction clear is the foundation of this entire unit.

Protein — Functions, Sources and Quality

Protein builds and repairs muscle, makes enzymes and hormones, and supports immune function. The body breaks protein down into amino acids. Of the 20 amino acids in food, nine are essential — we cannot make them ourselves and must eat them. This is where high biological value (HBV) protein comes in. Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, and soya beans all supply HBV protein. In contrast, most plant proteins (beans, lentils, nuts, cereals) are low biological value (LBV) — they’re missing at least one essential amino acid.

Key Fact

HBV proteins (meat, fish, eggs, dairy, soya) contain all nine essential amino acids. LBV proteins (beans, lentils, most cereals) are missing at least one. Vegetarians and vegans can meet all amino acid needs by combining LBV sources.

Protein Complementation

Protein complementation means combining two or more LBV protein sources in the same meal so that the amino acids missing from one are supplied by the other. The classic examples are beans on toast (haricot beans + wheat), rice and peas (rice + kidney beans), and hummus and pitta (chickpeas + wheat). For a vegan teenager eating no animal products, this technique is essential to avoid protein deficiency.

Protein Alternatives

The spec names four main protein alternatives for vegetarian and vegan diets. TVP (textured vegetable protein) is made from defatted soya flour; it absorbs flavour well and can replace mince in a bolognese. Soya is the only plant food that is naturally HBV. Mycoprotein (sold as Quorn) is made from a fungus and is high in fibre as well as protein. Tofu is set soya curd; it has a neutral flavour and takes on marinades readily when diced for a stir-fry.

Students often write that plant proteins are “bad” or “incomplete” and leave it there. This misses the point. LBV proteins are perfectly healthy — they are simply missing one or more essential amino acids on their own. By using complementation (beans on toast, rice and peas, lentil soup with a bread roll), a vegan or vegetarian can get every essential amino acid they need without eating any animal products. Soya is actually HBV and is nutritionally equivalent to meat protein in that respect.

Deficiency and Excess

Protein deficiency is rare in the UK but causes kwashiorkor in severe cases (muscle wasting, swollen abdomen, poor immunity). Mild deficiency leads to slow growth in children and poor wound healing. Excess protein is not stored — the nitrogen is excreted as urea, putting extra strain on the kidneys. Most UK adults consume more protein than the Reference Nutrient Intake (RNI) of around 0.75 g per kg body weight per day.

Fats — Types, Functions and Effects

Fats supply more than twice the energy of protein or carbohydrate per gram (9 kcal/g versus 4 kcal/g). They insulate the body, protect organs, carry fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, and are essential for hormone production. There are two main types.

Saturated fats are solid at room temperature. Think butter, lard, the white fat on a lamb chop, the cream in a dessert. High intake raises LDL (“bad”) cholesterol, which is a risk factor for coronary heart disease (CHD). Current guidelines recommend that saturated fats make up no more than 11% of daily energy intake.

Unsaturated fats are liquid at room temperature and come in two sub-types: monounsaturated (olive oil, avocado, rapeseed oil) and polyunsaturated (sunflower oil, oily fish, walnuts). Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats can reduce LDL cholesterol. Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) are particularly rich in omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, which support heart health.

A common exam error is to write “fat is bad” and then list butter as the only source. Remember: unsaturated fats are essential. Without them, you cannot absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, and you risk deficiency of those nutrients too. The exam expects you to distinguish between saturated and unsaturated, name sources of each, and link saturated fat excess to CHD via raised LDL cholesterol. Fat deficiency — though rare — causes poor absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, dry skin, hormonal disruption and lack of energy.

Carbohydrates — Structure, Functions and Fibre

Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred energy source, supplying 4 kcal per gram. They come in three structural forms:

  • Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) — the simplest sugars; absorbed directly into the blood.
  • Disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose) — two monosaccharides joined together.
  • Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, dietary fibre (NSP)) — long chains of monosaccharides.

Starch is found in bread, pasta, rice, potatoes, cereals and oats. It is the slow-release fuel that should form the majority of a GCSE student’s energy intake. Free sugars (those added to food or naturally present in honey, syrups and fruit juices) should make up no more than 5% of total energy intake. Dietary fibre keeps the gut healthy, prevents constipation and reduces the risk of bowel cancer and type 2 diabetes.

Key Fact

Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose), disaccharides (sucrose), polysaccharides (starch, dietary fibre). Excess free sugars cause tooth decay and contribute to obesity and type 2 diabetes. The recommended maximum for free sugars is 5% of total energy intake.

Deficiency of carbohydrates means the body switches to fat then protein for fuel, producing ketone bodies, which can cause fatigue, brain fog and, in extreme cases, a dangerous condition called ketoacidosis. Deficiency of dietary fibre causes constipation and increases the long-term risk of bowel cancer. Excess carbohydrate (especially refined sugars) is stored as body fat once glycogen stores are full, contributing to obesity.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about macronutrients, the most common error is listing sources without giving any reasons. The command word “Explain” means “give reasons for and/or causes of” — so you must use linking words such as “because”, “this means that” or “as a result”. For example, if asked why a vegan diet might be low in HBV protein: “A vegan diet avoids all animal products, because of this it may be low in HBV protein (which contains all nine essential amino acids). This means that the vegan must combine LBV sources such as beans and bread so that the missing amino acids are supplied by the complementary food.” Two developed chains of reasoning like this typically reach the top marks. For the 6-mark Explain capstone, aim for two or three well-developed points, each with an example linked to the named dish or eater in the question — not six brief bullet points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Macronutrients (protein, fats and carbohydrates) provide energy; micronutrients do not. For every macronutrient the exam expects: functions, main sources, effects of deficiency and excess, and related dietary reference values.
  • HBV proteins (meat, fish, eggs, dairy, soya) contain all nine essential amino acids; LBV proteins (most plant foods) are missing one or more. Protein complementation — combining two LBV sources — is essential for vegans.
  • Saturated fats (solid, mainly animal sources) raise LDL cholesterol and increase CHD risk; unsaturated fats (liquid, plant and fish sources) are healthier alternatives. Excess free sugars (monosaccharides and disaccharides added to food) cause tooth decay and obesity; dietary fibre protects gut health.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following foods is a source of high biological value (HBV) protein?
A. Brown rice
B. Kidney beans
C. Lentils
D. Eggs
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for D (Eggs). Rice, kidney beans and lentils are all LBV protein sources.

practice_questions.text: State two protein alternatives suitable for a vegan diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: TVP (textured vegetable protein); soya; mycoprotein (Quorn); tofu. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by protein complementation and give one example of how it is used in a meal.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that protein complementation means combining two or more LBV protein sources; 1 mark for explaining that this supplies all essential amino acids that would be missing from one source alone; 1 mark for a named example (e.g. beans on toast / rice and peas / lentil soup with bread / hummus and pitta). Up to 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Priya is 15 and has recently become vegan. Her parents are concerned she may not be getting enough protein. Explain two steps Priya could take to meet her protein needs on a vegan diet.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks available per developed explanation (1 for the point, 1 for the developed reason or consequence). Examples: (1) Use protein complementation — combining two LBV sources such as beans on toast, because together they supply all nine essential amino acids that a single LBV source is missing. (2) Include soya products (tofu, edamame, soya milk) because soya is the only naturally HBV plant protein and will supply all essential amino acids without needing complementation. (3) Use mycoprotein or TVP as meat substitutes, because these are manufactured to have a comparable amino acid profile to meat and supply adequate protein. 1 mark for identification; 1 mark for developed reasoning, per point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the health effects of consuming a diet high in saturated fat over a long period of time.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. 1 mark for identifying that saturated fat raises LDL (bad) cholesterol; 1 mark for explaining that raised LDL causes narrowing/blocking of arteries (atherosclerosis); 1 mark for linking this to an increased risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) or stroke/heart attack. Award marks for any three accurate, distinct points.

practice_questions.text: Caitlin is a food technology teacher. She is planning a lesson to show students how to adapt a traditional beef lasagne recipe for a vegan family. Explain how Caitlin could adapt the protein sources in the lasagne while ensuring the dish still provides adequate protein for growth and repair in the teenage students who will eat it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies at least two protein substitutes (e.g. TVP or lentils for mince; cashew or soya-based cheese for dairy cheese) and explains how each works in the dish and why it provides adequate protein (TVP absorbs the tomato sauce flavour and supplies a protein profile similar to meat once fortified; lentils are LBV but when combined with wheat pasta achieve complementation; soya-based cheese is HBV). Sustained application to the teenage growth context (growth requires adequate essential amino acid supply for muscle and tissue repair). Accurate use of HBV/LBV/complementation vocabulary throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one substitute with development, or two substitutes with limited development. Some reference to adequate protein or growth context. Mostly accurate.

Developing (2 marks): Names a substitute without explaining how it provides adequate protein, or gives a general statement about vegan diets being low in protein without applying it to the lasagne scenario.

Emerging (1 mark): Very basic or partially relevant response, e.g. 'use tofu instead of meat' with no development or nutritional reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of fat is most strongly linked to raising LDL cholesterol and increasing the risk of coronary heart disease?
A student combines rice and kidney beans in the same meal. Which nutritional principle does this demonstrate?
Dietary fibre is a type of _____, which adds bulk to stools and helps maintain a healthy gut.
Soya is unusual among plant foods because it is a _____ protein, meaning it contains all nine essential amino acids.
Match each macronutrient with its correct energy value per gram.

flashcard_questions.a: A nutrient needed in large amounts that provides the body with energy.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a high biological value (HBV) protein?
flashcard_questions.a: A protein containing all nine essential amino acids; found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy and soya.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a low biological value (LBV) protein?
flashcard_questions.a: A protein missing one or more essential amino acids; found in most plant foods.
Combining two LBV protein sources in one meal to supply all nine essential amino acids.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of protein complementation in a meal.
flashcard_questions.a: Beans on toast — beans and wheat together supply all essential amino acids.

flashcard_questions.q: Which plant protein is naturally high biological value?
What health risk is linked to a long-term high intake of saturated fat?
flashcard_questions.a: Raised LDL cholesterol, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two sources of unsaturated fat.
flashcard_questions.a: Olive oil and oily fish (also acceptable: avocado, sunflower oil, walnuts).

flashcard_questions.q: How many kilocalories does fat provide per gram?
What is the recommended maximum percentage of total energy from free sugars?
What is dietary fibre (NSP) and where is it found?
flashcard_questions.a: Indigestible plant polysaccharide that adds bulk to stools; sources include wholegrain bread, vegetables, pulses, fruit.

flashcard_questions.q: What condition is caused by severe protein deficiency in children?
flashcard_questions.a: Kwashiorkor — characterised by muscle wasting and swollen abdomen.

flashcard_questions.q: What is mycoprotein and what is its nutritional advantage?
flashcard_questions.a: A protein made from fungus (sold as Quorn); it is high in both protein and dietary fibre.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to excess carbohydrate once glycogen stores are full?
flashcard_questions.a: It is converted and stored as body fat, contributing to obesity.

glossary_terms.definition: Nutrients required in relatively large amounts that supply energy; the three macronutrients are protein, fats and carbohydrates.
A protein that contains all nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts; found in animal products and soya.
A protein that is missing or low in one or more of the nine essential amino acids; found in most plant foods.
Fats that are solid at room temperature, mainly from animal sources; high intake is linked to raised LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular disease.
The indigestible plant-based polysaccharide that adds bulk to stools, slows glucose absorption and feeds beneficial gut bacteria.
